intro: The finale of Brahms’s Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68 (Adagio — Più andante — Allegro non troppo, ma con brio — Più allegro) introduces a horn call, a quiet trombone chorale and a C-major string tune. The chorale returns in the final pages, played by brass and strings together.

sections.label: Intro · Adagio, C minor, pizzicato strings
sections.mNote: Slow phrases alternate with pizzicato figures that accelerate

sections.label: B · Horn call in C major
sections.mNote: Horn and flute above muted string tremolo

sections.label: C · Trombone chorale
sections.mNote: Bassoons support the brass; the horn call follows again

sections.label: A · C-major violin theme, Allegro non troppo
sections.mNote: Low strings play pizzicato beneath the Allegro melody

sections.label: A′ · Return of the tune, varied
sections.mNote: C major leads out towards E♭ and F♯

sections.label: D · Descending bass returns, winds and low strings
sections.mNote: Winds and low strings exchange the four-note descent.

sections.label: Coda · Faster strings and the chorale
sections.mNote: A quiet build-up leads to the Più allegro and C major.

cues.title: Opening descent, lower strings
cues.text: Violas, cellos and double basses begin a four-note descent. Above them the violins play a slow version of the melody that later returns as the main tune in C major. Here it is in C minor, and accelerating pizzicato strings interrupt it.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 1–11, Simrock first edition (1877), p. 43 onwards; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pizzicato passages in the introduction
cues.text: In the introduction all the strings play pizzicato. Two-note figures pass between the groups, starting very soft and growing faster and louder through G minor, E♭ minor and F minor, until a chord is suddenly cut off. A second pizzicato passage, shorter and faster, follows later.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 6–11 and 16–19: the two pizzicato passages of the Adagio; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horn call, Più andante
cues.text: The music moves to C major, and a horn plays the call. Muted violins and violas play a tremolo beneath the long notes, and the timpani roll softly. The tune passes between the horns, so the line continues without a break. The flutes take it up next.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, Più andante, bars 30–46; horn and flute statements, muted tremolo strings and timpani. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Birthday greeting to Clara Schumann, 1868
cues.text: In 1868 Brahms sent Clara Schumann a birthday greeting containing the melody that became this horn call. Eight years later he placed it at the turning point of his First Symphony.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel identifies the horn call as a birthday greeting to Clara Schumann from 1868. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Trombone chorale
cues.text: Trombones and bassoons play a short chorale. The trombones play for the first time in the symphony in this movement. The chorale is absent through the Allegro and returns with the full orchestra near the end.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 47–51 and 407–416; Hansen’s score guide. The trombones’ restriction to the finale is also noted by Mandel. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html; https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegro theme, violins
cues.text: Low in their range, the violins begin the broad tune in C major over plucked lower strings, and horns fill out the harmony. The phrase runs to seventeen bars. Its second half delays the cadence by one bar.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, Allegro non troppo, ma con brio, bars 62–78; seventeen-bar melody and scoring described by Hansen. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Resemblance to Beethoven’s Ninth
cues.text: The big C-major tune recalls the “Ode to Joy” in Beethoven’s Ninth. When Brahms was asked about the likeness, he is reported to have replied: “Yes indeed, and what’s more remarkable is that every jackass immediately hears it.”
cues.evidence: Malte Krasting, Berliner Philharmoniker programme note, quoting Brahms’s reply: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/johannes-brahms-symphony-no-1-in-c-minor-op-68 . Mandel on the resemblance: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Transition to G major
cues.text: A third statement of the big tune begins in the full orchestra and breaks off at once; only its opening three-note turn is kept. Running scales in strings and bassoons move towards G major, punctuated loudly by winds, brass and low strings.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 94–113: transition, with the theme fragmented to its opening turn and running scales; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alphorn call and second theme
cues.text: Flute and horn bring back the alphorn call from the introduction, the horn echoing the flute. The low strings then repeat the four-note descent that opened the movement, and above it the violins play a second tune that winds down, leaps back up and continues.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 114–131: alphorn call in flute and horn, then the second theme over a four-note descending ostinato; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Close of the exposition, E minor
cues.text: Violas begin a tremolo that grows louder. The strings join in a descending arch that leads to a dotted rhythm, with loud cadences from winds and brass. From bar 176 the full orchestra, trombones included, plays the extended cadence in E minor.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 142–185: closing material and extended E-minor cadence, with trombones from bar 176; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the main theme
cues.text: The broad tune returns in C major with a fuller accompaniment. Its continuation soon turns towards E♭ and then F♯.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 186–219; combined return and development. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Pizzicato passages, development
cues.text: In the development (bars 204–219), plucked figures pass from the violins to the low strings, as in the two pizzicato passages of the introduction. Horns and bassoons hold chords over them, and trumpets join as the passage builds. The key moves up to F♯ major, and the pizzicato starts again.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 204–219: counterstatement with pizzicato passages recalling the introduction; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Start of the development
cues.text: At the point where the transition began its running scales in the exposition, two bars of heavy accents in the strings break in. The scales then move to D minor, fully harmonised, and thin out. Above them, oboe and flute exchange fragments of the opening turn of the big tune.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 220–256: transition interrupted at bar 232, scales in D minor, turn figures in oboe and flute; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax with the horn call
cues.text: Winds play the turn figures of the main theme over brass chords and timpani rolls. At the climax the full orchestra plays descending figures from the horn call off the beat, in C minor, and the trombones enter for the first time since the exposition.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 268–288; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the horn call
cues.text: The horn call returns over smoothly moving violas and cellos. The tremolo strings of the introduction are absent. Violins extend the tune, then descend, marked calando — dying away.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 289–300; horn-call return and altered accompaniment. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the second theme
cues.text: The second theme returns in C major. Its four-note descending bass passes between the low strings and flute, clarinet and bassoon. The descent comes from the finale’s first bars.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 301–325; alternating wind and string statements of the descending ostinato. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing material in C minor
cues.text: In the exposition this closing material was in E minor; strictly transposed it would now be in A minor, but the symphony ends in C, so in bars 316–339 Brahms keeps it in C minor. The violas play tremolo, the strings descend in unison and loud cadences move towards B♭.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 316–339: closing material in C minor in place of the analogous A minor; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: American performances, 1877–1881
cues.text: Leopold Damrosch conducted the first American performance at New York’s Steinway Hall on 15 December 1877. Boston heard it on 3 January 1878 under Carl Zerrahn. The Boston Symphony Orchestra played it in its first season, on 10 December 1881, under Georg Henschel.
cues.evidence: Performance history in Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Transition to the coda
cues.text: Trombone, contrabassoon and low strings play the main theme in its darker form. Violin arpeggios rise above a timpani roll. The phrases shorten and speed up until seven hammered chords begin the Più allegro.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, transition to coda, bars 367–390; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più allegro, bars 391–406
cues.text: Più allegro, in cut time. The strings repeat three notes taken from the turn in the main theme, over the timpani. Against them the winds and brass play two diminished-seventh chords, and each one resolves.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 391–406: Più allegro, cut time, churning strings and diminished-seventh chords; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chorale reprise in the coda
cues.text: The quiet chorale from the introduction returns in brass and strings together. Around it, the strings play turning figures as the faster coda (bars 407–457) moves towards the final chords in C major.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, coda, bars 407–457; chorale reprise and C-major close. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars and final chords
cues.text: The churning figure returns under loud chords in the brass and wind, which work upward. The basses play a loud rising arpeggio over a timpani roll. The full orchestra then plays three short C-major chords and a long final chord over the roll.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 447–457: closing passage and final chords; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Più andante: horn call in C major
transitions.from: Intro · Adagio, C minor, pizzicato strings
transitions.to: B · Horn call in C major
transitions.how: The C-minor introduction breaks off. Low strings descend and diminish into Più andante. The horn call opens in C major over a soft timpani roll, with the trombones’ first entry. Muted violins and violas begin a tremolo beneath the tune.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 24–38; Hansen’s score guide and Simrock first edition, p. 48. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html

transitions.title: Horn call, trombone chorale, dominant preparation
transitions.from: B · Horn call in C major
transitions.how: The flutes finish the C-major horn melody. Trombones and bassoons follow with a short chorale in measured chords, and a timpani roll marks its final downward leap. The horns then take up the call again above string tremolo and build towards the dominant chord that prepares the Allegro.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 38–61; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Brass hold G before the violin theme
transitions.to: A · C-major violin theme, Allegro non troppo
transitions.how: Horn and trombone hold the dominant chord on G and the other instruments stop. The violins then enter low in their range with the broad C-major melody, accompanied by horns and by cellos and basses playing pizzicato. The marking is Allegro non troppo, ma con brio.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 52–78; Hansen’s score guide and Simrock first edition, p. 52. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html

transitions.title: Wind figures lead to the theme’s return
transitions.from: A · C-major violin theme, Allegro non troppo
transitions.to: A′ · Return of the tune, varied
transitions.how: After the cadence in E minor, quiet rising figures in the winds lead back to the broad violin tune in C major, now with a fuller accompaniment. The continuation moves towards E♭ and F♯, and the returned melody goes into another long development.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 176–219; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Horn call to the descending basses
transitions.from: A′ · Return of the tune, varied
transitions.to: D · Descending bass returns, winds and low strings
transitions.how: The horn call returns and broadens over moving strings. The violins extend it, then descend over pulsating timpani, marked calando. All the strings introduce the four-note descent of the second group in C major. Later statements alternate between the low strings and the flute, clarinet and bassoon.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 289–315; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: From the C-minor cadence to the coda
transitions.from: D · Descending bass returns, winds and low strings
transitions.to: Coda · Faster strings and the chorale
transitions.how: The C-minor closing cadence dies down, and horns, violins and clarinets play quiet rising figures over viola tremolo. Trombone, contrabassoon and low strings bring back the main tune above a long timpani roll. The violin arpeggios grow shorter and rise in pitch, and a stringendo leads into the faster C-major coda.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, IV, bars 360–391; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: IV. Adagio — Più andante — Allegro, pp. 43–100; horn call at bar 30, chorale at bar 47, Allegro at bar 62 and later returns. Bar references follow Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide.

timeline.note: Low strings descend four notes beneath a slow violin version of the coming Allegro tune.
All-string pizzicato figures pass between registers in the first accelerating interruption.
The Più andante introduces the horn call over quiet brass support, timpani and muted string tremolo.
Flutes take up the horn call above string tremolo, with a trumpet echo.
Trombones and bassoons play the short chorale, supported by contrabassoon and low horns.
The broad Allegro tune begins in strings over plucked lower strings and supporting horns.
Winds and violins exchange fragments of the broad tune as more brass join.
The second group sets its melodic line above the recurring four-note bass descent.
The broad violin tune returns in C major, supported by horns and answering winds.
The horn call returns above smoothly moving violas and cellos.
Low strings and winds exchange the four-note descending bass in C major.
The main tune returns in the low brass and strings beneath rising violin arpeggios and a timpani roll.
Brass and strings play the chorale together in the faster C-major coda.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
